body.text: Chinese Premier Li Qiang yesterday hailed the progress in relations between China and Southeast Asia despite the growing global trend of “unilateralism and protectionism,” pitching China as the global defender of free trade.

Speaking at the 29th ASEAN-China Summit in Manila, Li said that trade between China and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc had topped $1 trillion in 2025, up by more than 20 percent in 2021, while cumulative two-way investment exceeded $500 billion.

“The past five years have been truly extraordinary, and the achievements we scored have not come easily,” he said, according to the official translation of his comments. “We remain firmly committed to safeguarding multilateralism and promoting free trade and endeavor to make the pie bigger.”

Citing the growing protectionism and “recurring geopolitical conflicts on the global stage,” Li said that it was “all the more important for China and ASEAN to stand united, ward off interference, and work together.”

Li’s comments came just prior to U.S. President Donald Trump’s arrival in the Philippine capital, where he is scheduled to meet with ASEAN leaders and attend a brief meeting with leaders from the Quad, a security grouping that also includes Japan, Australia, and India.

With its implicit attack on the United States’ protectionist turn under the second Trump administration, Li’s comments were deliberately tuned to his hosts’ particular concerns about the current trajectory of U.S. foreign policy.

Trump’s tariff and trade policy has been among the primary points of tension in U.S.-Southeast Asia relations since Trump took office for the second time. ASEAN member states were among the nations hardest hit by Trump’s “liberation day” tariff announcement. Most have spent much of the 18 months since negotiating trade deals with Washington; some have pledged to begin diversifying their trade partnerships to reduce their reliance on the U.S. market.

Southeast Asia has been negatively impacted by the effects of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year, which exposed the dependence of most nations on imported oil and refined fuels from the Gulf. On top of this, the Trump administration’s staunch support for Israel, and its support for the Israeli assaults on Gaza, remains a subject of concern in Muslim-majority Southeast Asia.

Indeed, pro-enterprise and free trade arguments have been a staple of Chinese diplomatic engagements with Southeast Asia since the “liberation day” tariffs. During a state visit to Vietnam last April, less than two weeks after Trump’s bombshell announcement, President Xi Jinping argued that “there are no winners in a trade war” and called on his partners in Hanoi to “resolutely safeguard the multilateral trading system, stable global industrial and supply chains, and open and cooperative international environment.”

The theme was also prominent during last year’s ASEAN Summit and related meetings in Malaysia. During the ASEAN Plus Three Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Li called on his Asian counterparts to “uphold free trade and the multilateral trading system, oppose all forms of protectionism, and continuously advance regional economic integration.” The following day, China and ASEAN signed an upgrade to their free trade agreement, which came into force in 2010.

While Li was likely preaching to the choir, his hosannahs to the virtues of free trade are unlikely to efface the region’s longstanding concerns about China. These include concerns about China’s military buildup, both on land and at sea, and its industrial overcapacity, all of which lead the region to prioritize good relations with the U.S., despite the volatility of the Trump era.

For this week’s host, the Philippines – the one South China Sea claimant state that is also a U.S. treaty ally – the tension is particularly fraught. Over the past four years, the China Coast Guard has increased the frequency of its incursions into Philippine-claimed parts of the South China Sea. This has prompted a series of dangerous confrontations, some involving direct physical altercations between the two sides.

The maritime tensions also featured in yesterday’s meeting. In his address, Li called on both sides “us to build up strategic trust, properly handle differences through dialogue and negotiation, jointly oppose foreign interference, and uphold regional peace and stability.” He added that China “looks forward to the early adoption of a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, so as to provide solid institutional safeguards for lasting peace and stability in the South China Sea.”

The Code of Conduct is intended to reduce the risk of conflict in the important waterway, where China’s expansive “nine-dash line” maritime claim clashes with those of four ASEAN member states: the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Brunei. The Philippines had intended to conclude negotiations on the Code during its chairmanship this year, but this week announced that it had fallen short of this goal, despite securing agreement on around 80 percent of the draft agreement. Negotiations will continue next year under Singapore’s chairmanship of ASEAN.

The holdup on the Code, which has been under negotiation now for more than two decades, reflects the ongoing tensions in disputed waters, as well as fundamental differences – both between China and ASEAN and between ASEAN’s 11 member states. Among the most intractable differences are the geographic scope to be covered by the agreement and whether or not the Code should be legally binding.

According to a draft joint statement quoted by the Associated Press, Chinese and ASEAN leaders nonetheless pledged “to exercise self-restraint in the conduct of activities that would complicate or escalate disputes and affect peace and stability” in the disputed waters. The draft statement also welcomed the “positive momentum and significant progress” on the Code of Conduct and emphasized “the need to maintain and promote an environment conducive to the negotiations.”

It is hard to read too much into such statements, which are a perennial feature of ASEAN summit proceedings. The question is whether they translate into real compromise in the years to come, which based on the evidence of the past decades, seems unlikely.
